title: Too many Cainites
summary: Why the Holy City draws and strains the Damned.

claims.text: Cainites usually keep apart to avoid mortal suspicion and fights over feeding, but Jerusalem draws far too many of them.
Endless pilgrims, merchants and mercenaries mean nearly everyone can feed, yet no Cainite there feels safe, and the immortal city seethes with barely held conflict.

title: The Weeks of Blood
summary: The Cainite frenzy after the crusader capture of 1099.

claims.text: The crusader capture of Jerusalem in 1099 was followed by slaughter so great that some streets ran deep with blood.
The blood madness took the Cainites too: they tore victims apart without stopping to drink and fought one another openly in the streets.
Most were so lost in frenzy that they failed to seek shelter from the sun, and very few of the Cainites present survived.

title: Cainites under the Kingdom of Jerusalem
summary: How the city’s undead society was rebuilt after 1099.

claims.text: In 1120 the Brujah Azif came to the city and set about rotting its Christian institutions from within, aiming to bring down the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
Refugees from Etheria’s Bethlehem returned after the crusader capture, more easily if they were Christian than Jewish or Muslim.
Because mortal power now favoured Christians, Christian Cainites quickly settled behind most of the city’s key institutions, while Jewish and Muslim Cainites found them hard to penetrate.
The Nosferatu Ephraim Embraced Hannah, a crippled waif, around 1180.

title: Observant vampires
summary: Jewish and Muslim Cainites and the ban on blood.

claims.text: The hardest question for Jewish and Muslim Cainites is that their faiths forbid consuming blood, while Christian Cainites face no such rule.
Knowing the ban does not let them master the hunger, so each must make a private peace with God over breaking scripture.
Some Cainites argue that the scriptural prohibition does not apply to their kind.

title: Gabriel Chavez, the Eyes of Alamut

claims.text: Gabriel Chavez was born in 699 near Barcelona to an Iberian mother and an unknown Berber Muslim father.
Rejecting the maternal side of the family, Gabriel left home at the first chance to join the Umayyads and learn honour and the Qur’an.
Among the Cainites of Jerusalem, Gabriel serves as the Eyes of Alamut.
